'''''Parkinsonia aculeata''''' is a species of [[perennial]] [[Flowering plant|flowering]] [[tree]] in the [[pea]] family, [[Fabaceae]]. Common names include '''palo verde''', '''Mexican palo verde''', '''Parkinsonia''', '''Jerusalem thorn''', '''jelly bean tree''', '''palo de rayo''', and '''retama'''.<ref>[http://www.jp.gobierno.pr/Portal_JP/Portals/0/Documentos%20Ambientales/2012-121-044JP5AnejoEvaluacionAmbiental.pdf ''Construcción de Infraestructuras Mínimas Recreativas y Educativas en la Reserva Natural Punta Cucharas: Evaluación Ambiental: Punta Cucharas.''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160821101519/http://www.jp.gobierno.pr/Portal_JP/Portals/0/Documentos%20Ambientales/2012-121-044JP5AnejoEvaluacionAmbiental.pdf |date=2016-08-21 }} Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales de Puerto Rico. Page 17. October 2012. Accessed 21 February 2019.</ref>

==Etymology==
The genus name ''Parkinsonia'' honors the English botanist [[John Parkinson (botanist)|John Parkinson]] (1567–1650), while the species Latin name ''aculeata'' refers to the thorny stem of this plant.

The name "Jerusalem thorn" stems from a mistranslation of the Spanish/Portuguese word ''girasol'' ('turning toward the sun').<ref>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-year=1980 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0394507614 |edition=Chanticleer Press|page=499}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Parkinsonia aculeata 4.jpg|thumb|220px|Close-up on flowers of ''Parkinsonia aculeata'']] ''Parkinsonia aculeata'' may be a spiny shrub or a small tree. It grows {{convert|2|to|8|m|ft|abbr=on}} high, with a maximum height of {{convert|10|m}}. Palo verde may have single or multiple stems and many branches with pendulous leaves. The [[leaf|leaves]] and stems are [[trichome|hairless]]. The leaves are alternate and pennate (15 to 20 cm long). The flattened [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] is edged by two rows of 25–30 tiny oval leaflets; the leaflets are soon [[deciduous]] in dry weather (and during the winter in some areas) leaving the green petioles and branches to [[photosynthesis|photosynthesize]].

The branches grow double or triple sharp [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|spines]] {{convert|7|-|12|mm|in|abbr=on}} long at the axils of the leaves. The [[flower]]s are yellow- orange and fragrant, {{convert|20|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, growing from a long slender stalk in groups of eight to ten. They have  five sepals and five petals, four of them clearer and rhomboid ovate, the fifth elongated, with a warmer yellow and purple spots at the base. The flowering period is in the middle months of spring (March–April or September–October). The flowers are pollinated by bees. The [[fruit]] is a [[legume|seedpod]], leathery in appearance, light brown when mature.

==Invasive problems==
''P. aculeata'' is a major [[invasive species]] in [[Australia]], as it is listed as a [[Weeds of National Significance|Weed of National Significance]] and is ranked as Australia's worst weed. It is also a major problem in parts of tropical [[Africa]], [[Hawaii]], and other [[Pacific islands|Islands]] in the [[Pacific Ocean]].

It was introduced to Australia as an [[ornamental tree]] and for shade around 1900. It is now a serious [[Invasive species in Australia|weed]] widespread through [[Western Australia]], the [[Northern Territory]] and [[Queensland]], covering about {{convert|8000|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}} of land, and has the potential to spread through most of the [[Semi-arid climate|semi-arid]] to subhumid tropical area in Australia.

It forms dense [[thicket]]s, preventing access for humans, native animals and [[livestock]] to waterways. The fruits (seedpods) float, and the plant spreads by dropping pods into water, or pods are washed downstream by seasonal [[flood]]ing.  Without the scarifying received by tumbling in streambeds, the seeds are slow to germinate.

Several control methods are used to reduce the existing population and the spread of ''P. aculeata'' in Australia. Three [[insect]]s have been [[Introduced species|introduced]] to Australia for [[biological control]]; the parkinsonia [[bean weevil]]s, ''Penthobruchus germaini'' and ''Mimosestes ulkei'', both have [[larva]]e that specifically eat the seeds from parkinsonia pods and are proving to be a useful management tool, and the parkinsonia leaf bug, ''Rhinacloa callicrates'', which destroys [[photosynthesis|photosynthetic]] tissues but has had little overall impact on the plant. Fire is effective for young trees; mechanical removal and [[herbicide]]s are also used.

==Distribution==
''P. aculeata'' is native to the [[southwestern United States]] and northern [[Mexico]] south to [[Galápagos Islands|Galapagos Islands]] and northern [[Argentina]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=van Klinken|first1=Rieks|last2=Campbell|first2=Shane|last3=Heard|first3=Tim|last4=McKenzie|first4=John|last5=March|first5=Nathan|date=2009|title=The Biology of Australian Weeds: 54. 'Parkinsonia aculeata' L|journal=Plant Protection Quarterly|language=EN|volume=24|issue=3|pages=100–117|url=https://search.informit.org/doi/10.3316/ielapa.735077383474483}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Factsheet - Parkinsonia aculeata (Parkinsonia)|url=https://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/eafrinet/weeds/key/weeds/Media/Html/Parkinsonia_aculeata_(Parkinsonia).htm|access-date=2021-05-03|website=keys.lucidcentral.org}}</ref> It has been introduced in [[Africa]], [[Australia]], [[India]], [[Pakistan]] and [[Spain]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Salas|first1=José Blanco|last2=Pardo|first2=Francisco María Vázquez|date=2015|title=Parkinsonia aculeata L. (Caesalpiniaceae), una amenaza más para el medio ambiente de Extremadura (España)|url=|journal=Bouteloua|issue=21|pages=111–115|issn=1988-4257}}</ref>

==Habitat==
''Parkinsonia aculeata'' has a high tolerance to drought, simply attaining shorter stature. In moist and humus-rich environments it becomes a taller, spreading shade tree.  This plant prefers a full sun exposure, but can grow on a wide range of dry soils (sand dunes, clay, alkaline and chalky soils, etc.), at an altitude of {{convert|0|-|1500|m}} above sea level.

==Uses==
In Mexico, the leaves are steeped and made into medicine for fever and epilepsy.<ref name=Peattie>{{cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |author-link=Donald C. Peattie |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |year=1953 |publisher=[[Bonanza Books]] |location=New York |page=572}}</ref>

The foliage is seldom browsed by livestock due to the spines.<ref name=Peattie/>
